title: How Does GPS Know Where You Are?
note: Benchmark sample only. Facts are widely published but this script has not been through the fact-checking step and is not for upload.

scenes.narration: Right now, the phone in your pocket can work out where you are to within a few metres. And here is the strange part. It never sends a single message to space. It only listens. So how can a device that never talks to a satellite know exactly where it is standing? The answer is a story about clocks, distance, and a correction that comes straight from Einstein.

keyframes.title: How does GPS know where you are?
keyframes.subtitle: Clocks, distance, and a correction from Einstein

scenes.narration: GPS is a group of about thirty satellites run by the United States. They circle the Earth at roughly twenty thousand two hundred kilometres up, far higher than the International Space Station. Each one goes around the planet about twice a day. They are spread out so that, from almost anywhere on Earth, at least four of them are above the horizon at any moment.

keyframes.title: Why so many?
items: At least four visible from almost anywhere

scenes.narration: Every satellite broadcasts a simple message, over and over. It says two things. Here is exactly where I am in my orbit, and here is exactly what time it was when I sent this. That is all. The satellite does not know you exist. Your phone simply catches these messages as they arrive.

keyframes.title: What the satellite does not know

keyframes.label: messages your phone sends to GPS satellites

scenes.narration: Now comes the clever part. The signal travels at the speed of light, about three hundred thousand kilometres every second. If your phone knows when the message left the satellite, and when it arrived, it can multiply that travel time by the speed of light. The result is the distance to that satellite. For GPS, that trip takes less than a tenth of a second.

Knowing your distance from one satellite is not enough. It only tells you that you are somewhere on a giant sphere around that satellite. Picture it as a circle on a flat map. You could be anywhere on that line.

keyframes.title: One satellite: you are somewhere on this circle

scenes.narration: Add a second satellite, and you get a second circle. The two circles cross in only two places. Add a third, and only one point sits on all three circles. That point is you. This method is called trilateration, and it works because each distance removes a huge number of possible positions.

But there is a problem. All of this depends on time, and the clock in your phone is cheap. Light travels three hundred metres in a single microsecond. So if your phone's clock is off by just one thousandth of a second, every distance it calculates is wrong by about three hundred kilometres. That would put you in the wrong city.

keyframes.label: distance light travels in one microsecond

keyframes.title: Position error from a clock error
The weak link
items: Small time errors become huge distance errors

scenes.narration: The solution is elegant. Instead of trusting its own clock, the phone treats the clock error as one more unknown. Its position has three unknowns: east-west, north-south, and height. Add the clock error, and there are four. Four unknowns need four measurements, so the phone listens to at least four satellites and solves for all of them at once.

That is why the satellites carry atomic clocks. These clocks count the vibrations of atoms, which happen at an extremely steady rate. Because the whole system depends on them, GPS has quietly become one of the world's most important time sources. Phone networks, power grids and banks all use GPS time to stay in sync.

keyframes.title: Atomic clocks in orbit
items: Several clocks per satellite for backup

scenes.narration: And here is where Einstein comes in. Because the satellites move fast, their clocks run slightly slow, by about seven microseconds a day. But because they are farther from Earth's gravity, their clocks also run fast, by about forty five microseconds a day. Together, the satellite clocks gain about thirty eight microseconds every day. If engineers ignored this, GPS positions would drift by roughly ten kilometres a day. So the clocks are adjusted to account for relativity.

keyframes.title: The fix
items: Satellite clocks are tuned before launch

scenes.narration: Even with all of this, GPS is not perfect. The signal slows down slightly as it passes through the upper atmosphere. In cities, it bounces off tall buildings before reaching you. And if the visible satellites are bunched together in one part of the sky, small errors get bigger. This is why your location sometimes jumps around between skyscrapers.

keyframes.title: What makes GPS less accurate
items: Satellites bunched in one part of the sky

keyframes.label: tall buildings block and reflect signals

scenes.narration: So, every time you open a map, your phone is quietly listening to satellites twenty thousand kilometres away, timing their signals, turning time into distance, solving four equations, and correcting for Einstein. All of that happens in a moment, and it never says a word back.
